reason: Both give the same core strategy: reframe bloat as a cost, replace the checklist with timed hands-on evals, start in greenfield alongside the incumbent, and disqualify buyers who need the checklist. B adds the point not to sell "Incumbent Lite" but to own an architectural shift the incumbent can't retrofit. It also explains that checklists exist to price migration risk and give cover, and it gives a clearer disqualifier (procurement owns the rubric and devs have no veto). Its trap questions for champions are actionable. A's "ask why Feature X is required" and its warning that the incumbent wrote the RFP are good, but B is a little sharper strategically and more concise.
